title: Epic A — Produce the v0.1 planning package
body:
Execute `docs/planning/PLANNING-PROMPT.md` §9: thirteen self-contained, cross-referenced files under `docs/planning/v0.1/`. This is the blueprint the build phase executes without further architectural decisions.

Exit condition: the §11 self-review checklist passes on every item.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-planning-package`, `oac-evidence`, `oac-boundaries`

title: Epic B — Stage 0: evidence, pinning, and ADR amendments
body:
Pin every external version, re-verify the §3 baseline against those pins, and close the Appendix A conflict register with numbered ADR-001 amendments.

Gate: no substantial core or transport code starts before Stage 0 and Stage 1 complete.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-evidence`, `oac-boundaries`

title: Epic C — Architecture decisions (PLANNING-PROMPT §5)
body:
Every §5 decision recorded with the choice, the decisive evidence, rejected alternatives in one line each, and the condition that would reverse it. No routine choice may be left as an open alternative. Decisions land in `docs/planning/v0.1/03-decisions-and-amendments.md`.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-evidence`, `oac-boundaries`

title: Epic D — Stage 1: gates G1-G5 and protocol fixtures
milestone: M2 — Stage 1: Provider and transport spikes
body:
Throwaway, timeboxed spikes that decide the five gates and capture recorded protocol fixtures for the Stage 3 fakes. Risk-first: nothing durable is built until the provider surfaces are proven on pinned versions.

Every gate produces a written result with version, date, command transcript summary, and verdict. Gates re-run whenever a pinned provider version changes.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-gates`, `oac-evidence`

title: Epic E — Stage 2: normative OAC spec v0.1
body:
The neutral specification and its conformance fixtures. Interfaces (adapter contract, transport contract, core types) are frozen at the end of this stage.

Hard rule: no neutral interface or spec text mentions Zenoh keys, MQTT topics, NATS subjects, or provider-specific method names.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-spec-authoring`, `oac-boundaries`

title: Epic F — Stage 3: core, fakes, and contract suites
body:
Core types, policy, identity, duplicate suppression, fake Claude and fake Codex endpoints built from Stage 1 fixtures, an in-memory transport, and the contract test suites.

Exit condition: CI green with no live provider, no API key, and no network beyond loopback.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-implementation`, `oac-testing`, `oac-boundaries`

title: Epic G — Stage 4: provider adapters and Zenoh transport
milestone: M5 — Stage 4: Adapters and Zenoh transport
body:
Real adapters and the reference transport, built against the contracts frozen in Stage 2. Contract suites pass on the real modules; provider integration tests pass on pinned versions behind an explicit opt-in.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-implementation`, `oac-claude-channels`, `oac-codex-appserver`, `oac-zenoh`, `oac-boundaries`

title: Epic H — Stage 5: end-to-end and threat verification
milestone: M6 — Stage 5: End-to-end and threat verification
body:
The ADR-001 validation criterion executed on Windows, macOS, and Linux, plus the security test suite. Each of DESIGN acceptance criteria 1-10 maps to a named passing test; each threat-model mitigation maps to the test that proves it.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-testing`, `oac-security-work`

title: Epic I — Stage 6: release hygiene
body:
Docs, license inventory, deferred-work list, known-risk list, and upgrade notes for provider preview surfaces.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-release`, `oac-evidence`

title: Epic J — Progressive-disclosure agent skills
body:
A tiered skill tree so an agent picking up any work item loads the minimum context needed: an always-on router, two guardrail skills, one skill per stage, and four provider/transport reference skills. See `docs/planning/SKILLS-MODEL.md`.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-authoring-skills`

title: Epic K — herdr-driven harness verification tooling
body:
Test-side tooling that drives real Claude Code and Codex CLI sessions through herdr (Apache-2.0 terminal multiplexer with a CLI/socket API) so gate re-runs and opt-in provider-integration/end-to-end runs can be scripted instead of requiring a human operator at the keyboard. herdr is dev/test tooling only: never imported by or shipped in `adapters/`, `core/`, `cli/`, or `transports/`; never CI-default; never a substitute for a supported interface (ADR-001 boundary 4/13). Human-operated gate spikes remain the authoritative method; G1-G4 verdicts are unchanged.

Exit condition: one gate re-run end to end by the driver with a fixture equivalent to the human-run one, a passing herdr-in-product-paths lint, and an opt-in CI job on an operator-owned runner.

**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-testing`, `oac-gates`, `oac-boundaries`, `oac-evidence`

title: Epic L — Beacon (agent-beacon) as an external shared-memory layer beside OAC sessions
body:
**Milestone (proposed):** none yet — the decision record (L1) and the desk research (L2) can run now, in parallel with Stage 1, exactly as Epic K did. Everything that touches `spec/`, `adapters/*`, `cli/` or the test tiers is gated behind the stage that owns those paths (see "Dependencies").
**Labels:** `epic`, `type:decision`, `area:spec`, `area:security`
**Skills:** `oac`, `oac-boundaries`, `oac-evidence`, `oac-security-work`, `oac-spec-authoring` (L3 only), `oac-mcp` (L3 only), `oac-testing` (L6 only)

## Summary

The user goal is "integrate Beacon as a shared context layer": OAC manages several harness sessions and passes messages between them, and a persistent memory all of those sessions can reach should help them coordinate.

This epic scopes that goal so it stays inside ADR-001. **Beacon is an external, independently installed, review-gated memory service that each harness connects to natively over MCP. OAC never stores, fetches, summarizes, or injects memory.** OAC's role is limited to: a recorded decision that says so; a small, optional, provider-neutral way to *reference* a Beacon memory item from a Session Channels message; the security doctrine and threat-table rows that govern memory references and Beacon's capture of OAC-delivered messages; opt-in config/doctor/doc touchpoints; conformance fixtures; and an opt-in integration test. It is a decision + spec touchpoint + thin wiring epic, sized to a repository that is still in Stage 1 with no product code under `core/`, `spec/`, `adapters/` or `cli/` yet.

The literal reading of the goal — OAC itself becoming the shared context layer — is a boundary violation and is scoped out below, with the amendment route named in case the operator wants it anyway.

## Background: what agent-beacon is (first-party evidence)

All facts below were read from a `--depth 1` clone of the repository at its default-branch head, plus its tag list, on 2026-09-29. Retrieval date for every citation: **2026-09-29**.

- **Repository and pin candidates.** `https://github.com/Asymptote-Labs/agent-beacon`, default branch head commit `26581914e86f525e225096613c3a9b808043ff85` (committed 2026-09-29). Latest release tag `v1.3.29` (tag object `72fd6643b5cd5c6ff6741f6016b3577654f61915` → commit `91e92216b79108475ba9b587d49c5ff3f7356fd8`). Source: `git ls-remote --tags` on the repository, retrieved 2026-09-29. The L1 decision record pins one of these; this epic does not.
- **License.** MIT, "Copyright (c) 2026 Asymptote Labs". Source: `LICENSE` at commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29. Compatible with OAC's own Apache-2.0 for a doc-and-config-level integration; nothing from Beacon is vendored or linked by this epic.
- **What it is.** "Beacon is an open-source memory layer for AI coding agents that learns from your work across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and 20+ other harnesses. It captures full session history, identifies useful workflows, corrections, and debugging patterns, and makes that knowledge reusable by future agents." Source: `README.md` §"Beacon Overview", commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **Implementation.** A Go CLI (`cli/beacon/go.mod`, `cli/beacon/main.go`) plus a `cli/beacon-hooks` adapter binary; packaged via Homebrew, `.deb`/`.rpm`, and an MSI. Source: repository tree at commit `26581914`, `README.md` §"Quick Start", retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **Capture path per harness (the part that interacts with OAC).** README "Local Agent Coverage" table lists Claude Code as `OTLP + hooks + poll` and Codex CLI as `OTLP + hooks + poll`. Source: `README.md` §"Supported Agents", commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29. Consequence: **an OAC channel message delivered into a Beacon-instrumented session is, by construction, inside the session history Beacon captures** — see the threat workstream.
- **Interface: two MCP servers, distinct names.** (1) Local server `beacon`, started by `beacon mcp serve` over `--transport stdio|http`; HTTP is loopback JSON-RPC at default `--addr 127.0.0.1:8766`, endpoints `/mcp` and `/health`; the docs warn "Do not bind HTTP transport to a non-loopback interface." (2) Cloud server `beacon-managed`, registered by `beacon mcp connect` in "Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI and OpenCode", OAuth by default, read-only, tools `beacon_search_sessions`, `beacon_grep`, `beacon_read_session`, `beacon_get_event`, `beacon_lookup`, `beacon_usage`. Source: `docs/cli/mcp.mdx`, `docs/cli/mcp-serve.mdx`, `docs/cli/mcp-connect.mdx`, commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **Local MCP tool surface (verbatim).** `search_activity`, `summarize_activity`, `get_activity_event`, `list_activity_filters`, `search_memory`, `get_memory`, `get_memory_context`. "Memory tools read approved project memory only. They do not run Jev, approve candidates, install Agent Skills, or expose pending/rejected candidates." Source: `docs/cli/mcp.mdx` §"MCP tools", commit `26581914`; tool names also appear verbatim in `cli/beacon/internal/mcpserver/server.go`, retrieved 2026-09-29. **There is no MCP write path into memory** — writes go through the `beacon memory` CLI and are human-review-gated.
- **Memory model.** Durable local store `memory.db` "next to the endpoint runtime log base directory"; "Approved memory is scoped to the resolved project. Cross-project or user-global memory is not automatic."; candidate kinds `workflow`, `correction`, `debugging_pattern`, `gotcha`, `convention`; candidates come from an optional external evaluator (TypeSafe Jev, `beacon memory evaluations run`, opt-in, never from hooks) or from `beacon memory candidates create`; approval is an explicit CLI action. Approved memory can be rendered as an Agent Skill whose frontmatter carries provenance keys `beacon_memory_id`, `beacon_candidate_id`, `beacon_memory_kind`, `beacon_tags`. Source: `docs/concepts/cross-harness-memory.mdx`, `docs/cli/memory.mdx`, commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **How a harness connects.** Natively, as an ordinary MCP server entry the harness owns: the documented stdio entry is `{"mcpServers":{"beacon":{"command":"beacon","args":["mcp","serve","--transport","stdio"]}}}`; the Beacon plugin (`/plugin marketplace add asymptote-labs/agent-beacon`, `codex plugin marketplace add asymptote-labs/agent-beacon`) also registers the local server and installs the `beacon-memory-recall` / `beacon-memory-distill` / `beacon-memory-promote` skills. Source: `docs/cli/mcp-doctor.mdx` §"Client configuration", `docs/concepts/beacon-skills.mdx` §"Install", commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **Identity/scoping model.** Project-scoped by resolved repository path (`--project <path>` override; a linked worktree resolves to its main checkout); `search_memory`/`get_memory_context` take `project_id`, and "a `project` path sent by a client is matched against the projects the memory store already holds records for ... an unrecognized path returns nothing rather than widening the search." No per-agent or per-session identity inside memory: **Beacon has no notion of OAC's `Security principal -> Device -> Harness -> Session` hierarchy**, and it does not authenticate the MCP client on the local server beyond process/loopback locality. Source: `docs/cli/mcp.mdx`, `docs/cli/memory.mdx`, commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **Security posture.** Loopback-only OTLP receivers on `127.0.0.1`; secret redaction, sanitization, truncation and event-size limits before write; `runtime.jsonl` rotates at 10 MiB with five archives; forwarding (Beacon Cloud, SIEMs) is opt-in and customer-configured; "hooks never touch the network". Source: `SECURITY.md`, commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29.
- **MCP era.** The local server's `initialize` result advertises `"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05"` (`cli/beacon/internal/mcpserver/server.go` line 211, commit `26581914`, retrieved 2026-09-29). Informational only: this is Beacon-to-harness, not an OAC surface, and does not touch gate G4.

Surface labels (per `oac-evidence` §4): the `beacon` local MCP server and the `beacon memory` CLI are **supported** (documented in Beacon's own docs); `beacon-managed` / Beacon Cloud is **supported** but hosted and account-bound and is out of this epic's scope; the memory feature is documented as "opt-in" — treat its stability as **UNVERIFIED** until L1 pins a release and re-reads the docs at that tag.

**UNVERIFIED (to be closed or listed in L1/L2):**
- Whether Beacon's Claude Code capture (hooks/OTLP) records the content of an OAC channel notification delivered into the session, or only the harness-visible tool/prompt events (UNVERIFIED — no first-party statement found; matters for the threat rows).
- The exact shape and stability of the memory item ID and of `get_memory` / `get_memory_context` results across releases (UNVERIFIED — docs show flags and provenance keys but not a versioned response schema).
- Whether one `memory.db` can be shared by several harness sessions concurrently without a documented locking model (UNVERIFIED — not stated; likely fine for read-only MCP access but unstated).
- Whether Beacon's `codex` hook integration touches `~/.codex/config.toml` in a way that conflicts with OAC's Codex adapter launch (UNVERIFIED — `beacon mcp connect` documents an atomic text-only edit, but the endpoint hook install path was not examined).

## ADR-001 boundary analysis — the part that decides the shape

Quoted boundaries this goal runs up against:

- `[ADR-001 Boundary]` "MUST NOT ... implement inference/model routing/context management."
- `[DESIGN Non-goals]` "shared context management".
- `[PLANNING-PROMPT §10]` "Do not turn OAC into an agent framework, inference router, shared context manager, or provider-auth abstraction."
- `oac-boundaries` #12's drift example, verbatim: "a 'conversation memory' store shared across both providers so replies can reference earlier turns from either harness — that is a shared context manager."
- `[ADR-001 v0.1 scope]` defers "durable offline mailboxes" and "attachments".
- `[ADR-001 Boundary]` "MUST NOT steal or reuse another harness's provider credentials" — read here as also covering any Beacon Cloud OAuth session a harness holds.
- `[ADR-001 Boundary]` "MUST NOT leak Zenoh-specific concepts into the neutral protocol."

**Verdict.** "Integrate Beacon as a shared context layer *of OAC*" — OAC reading `memory.db`, calling `get_memory_context` on a session's behalf, attaching memory to envelopes, summarizing history, or choosing a recipient based on what memory says — is a shared context manager and is **out of bounds without an ADR-001 amendment**. This epic does not propose that amendment. If the operator wants it, the route is `oac-evidence` §6: record the conflict, cite evidence, and propose the next free `ADR-001-A<n>` with old text / new text / rationale, before any code.

**What stays in bounds — the chosen shape, "Beacon beside OAC, not inside it":**

1. **Beacon is a peer service each harness reaches natively.** Claude Code and Codex connect to `beacon mcp serve` through their own MCP configuration (or Beacon's plugin). That is the ADR-001 MAY clause in action — "documented MCP extensions ... or other supported IPC" — used by the *harness*, not by OAC. OAC does not launch, configure, proxy, or speak to Beacon's MCP server, and does not vendor or link any Beacon code.
2. **Memory stays in the harness's context, owned by the harness.** Recall happens when a harness runs `beacon-memory-recall` / `get_memory_context` in its own turn. OAC delivers only what a sender put in an envelope. No enrichment, no trimming, no summarization, no injection.
3. **OAC's only protocol touchpoint is a reference, not the content.** A sender that wants a peer to look something up may say so. The L1 decision picks between: (a) nothing in the spec — memory IDs are ordinary text in `content[].text` and this epic is docs-only; or (b) an optional, provider-neutral **memory-reference content entry** (working name only, fixed by L3) whose shape is a stable string ID plus a free-form `source` tag — never a Beacon-only type name, never a `project_id`-derived path, never fetched or validated by OAC. Both options are forward-compatible by `05-interfaces.md` §3's rule that "a receiver `MUST` ignore an array entry whose `type` it does not recognize." Option (b) must pass the neutral-vocabulary ban (`oac-spec-authoring`): it may not mention Beacon, `memory.db`, `get_memory_context`, or Zenoh.
4. **Authenticated but untrusted, extended to memory.** Under `06-security.md` §3(e) and the doctrine in §2/§8-§10, a memory reference in an envelope is *content*: a claim by the sender, rendered inside the untrusted body, never as provenance. The receiving harness resolves it through its own Beacon connection, and whatever Beacon returns is untrusted text to that harness as well — Beacon's own skill already says "It treats memory as lessons from earlier sessions, not as policy." OAC must never render a memory ID or a memory body in the machine-set provenance block.
5. **No credential handling.** OAC never holds Beacon Cloud OAuth tokens or `--token-env` personal tokens; `beacon-managed` is out of scope.
6. **No durable-mailbox side door.** Beacon's `search_activity` over `runtime.jsonl` must not be used as a way to "catch up on missed messages" — that is the deferred offline mailbox plus application-level polling (`[DESIGN Delivery semantics]`). Say so in the docs.
7. **Transport containment is unaffected.** Nothing here touches `transports/zenoh/`; the neutral protocol gains at most one optional, transport-agnostic content entry.

## In scope

- A decision record (`docs/planning/decisions/L1-beacon-memory.md`, name to be confirmed by house style) that fixes the shape above, pins one Beacon release, records the license under a "not shipped, external service" heading, and either closes or lists every UNVERIFIED item above.
- The spec touchpoint decision (option (a) vs (b) in point 3) and, if (b), the normative text plus conformance fixtures, landed in Stage 2.
- Threat-table rows and doctrine text for: memory references as untrusted content; Beacon's capture of OAC-delivered messages (cross-project disclosure, credential/secret leakage via `runtime.jsonl` and opt-in forwarding); a peer that cites a memory ID to lend false authority to an instruction.
- Documentation: a "running OAC sessions with Beacon on both sides" walkthrough that uses only Beacon's own install/connect commands and OAC's own launch commands; the explicit statement of what OAC does *not* do with memory.
- Optional, opt-in `oac doctor`-style detection ("Beacon local MCP server configured for harness X: yes/no") **only if** it can be done by reading the harness's own MCP configuration read-only, the same way `beacon mcp status` does — to be decided in L1, default no.
- An opt-in end-to-end scenario (Stage 5, via Epic K's driver) showing a memory reference travelling Claude → Codex and being resolved by the receiver's own Beacon connection.

## Out of scope (boundary, not backlog)

- OAC reading or writing `memory.db`, calling any `beacon` MCP tool, running `beacon` as a subprocess, bundling or vendoring Beacon, or adding a Beacon workspace dependency.
- Auto-attaching memory to outbound messages, injecting recall results into inbound messages, summarizing session history, or routing on memory content (`[ADR-001 Boundary]` context management; `oac-boundaries` #2, #8, #12).
- Any OAC-held Beacon Cloud or Jev credential (`[ADR-001 Boundary]` credential reuse; DESIGN "Replacement provider auth").
- Using Beacon's activity log or dashboard as a delivery, presence, or catch-up mechanism (deferred offline mailbox; no-polling rule).
- Beacon Cloud / `beacon-managed`, SIEM forwarding, and the browser extension.
- A Beacon-specific adapter, transport, or content type name in the neutral spec.
- Writing memory on a peer's behalf (there is no MCP write path anyway, and review-gating is Beacon's design, not something OAC bypasses).

## Workstreams (not tasks — a later pass decomposes these)

| # | Workstream | Stage / gate | Skills |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | **Decision record**: shape above fixed; Beacon release pinned (`docs/planning/PINS.md` row `Beacon (external memory service)`, `Gates affected: none`); MIT license recorded in `07-repository-and-dependencies.md` under an external-service, not-shipped heading; option (a)/(b) chosen; UNVERIFIED list closed or carried to `11-risks.md` and STATUS.md. | Now (like K1) | `oac-evidence`, `oac-boundaries`, `oac-security-work` |
| L2 | **Timeboxed research spike** (desk first; live leg herdr-driven, run locally by an agent — #187, 2026-09-30): confirm the four UNVERIFIED items against the pinned tag; capture what Beacon records when an OAC channel message lands in a Claude Code session and a Codex session (redacted fixture); confirm no config-file collision with OAC's launch paths. No product code. | Now; live leg needs a logged-in harness | `oac-gates` (timebox/fixture rules), `oac-evidence` |
| L3 | **Spec touchpoint** (only if L1 picks option (b)): optional content entry, neutral vocabulary, `MUST ignore if unrecognised`, conformance fixtures under the Stage 2 fixture format. | Stage 2 (Epic E) — blocked until Stage 1 exits | `oac-spec-authoring`, `oac-mcp`, `oac-boundaries` |
| L4 | **Security**: threat-table rows (attack / precondition / mitigation / proving test / residual) in `06-security.md` §14 and later `spec/security.md`; doctrine sentence that memory references and resolved memory are untrusted content; explicit "never in the provenance block" rule. | Doc rows now; normative text Stage 2; proving tests Stage 5 | `oac-security-work` |
| L5 | **Config, doctor, and docs**: walkthrough; the "what OAC does not do" statement; optional read-only doctor check if L1 allows it. | Docs now; any `cli/` change Stage 4 (Epic G) | `oac-release`, surface skills |
| L6 | **Tests**: opt-in integration scenario through `tools/herdr/` (Epic K reuse contract); CI-default tier unchanged; fixtures redacted per the gates README. | Stage 5 (Epic H) | `oac-testing`, `oac-gates` |
| L7 | **Agent enablement**: a short `references/beacon.md` under an existing skill (probably `oac-security-work` or `oac-release`), not a new surface skill, so future agents know the shape and the boundary. | After L1 | `oac-authoring-skills` |

Dependency order: L1 → {L2, L4-rows, L5-docs, L7} → L3 (Stage 2) → L5-cli (Stage 4) → L6 (Stage 5).

## Acceptance criteria (epic level)

1. A decision record exists that quotes the boundary lines above, states the chosen shape, and lists the rejected reading (OAC as context layer) with the amendment route named. Boundary self-check per `oac-boundaries` "Pre-commit self-check" passes on it.
2. One Beacon release is pinned in `docs/planning/PINS.md` with `Gates affected: none`; its MIT license is recorded; every Beacon fact in the record carries URL + commit/tag + retrieval date; every unresolved fact is labelled UNVERIFIED and mirrored in STATUS.md and `11-risks.md`.
3. The mechanical boundary checks (`oac-boundaries` `references/mechanical-checks.md`) show zero Beacon references under `core/`, `spec/` (other than the neutral content entry, if chosen), `adapters/*`, `transports/`, and `cli/` (other than an optional read-only doctor line), and no new workspace dependency.
4. If option (b) is chosen: the spec text names no vendor, product, tool, path, or transport; a conformance fixture proves an unrecognised content entry is ignored, not rejected; the entry is absent from the signed provenance block.
5. `06-security.md` §14 gains rows for the three threats above, each with a named proving test or an explicit "open risk" entry — no blank "proving test" cells.
6. The walkthrough runs with only Beacon's documented commands and OAC's documented launch commands; nowhere does OAC call, spawn, or configure Beacon.
7. No existing gate verdict, pin, or ADR text changes as a result of this epic.

## Risks and open questions (for the operator)

- **Q1 — option (a) or (b)?** Docs-only (memory IDs as plain text) is zero spec surface and zero risk; the typed content entry is cleaner for tooling but is a permanent v0.1 spec commitment made before Stage 2 opens. Recommendation: decide in L1; default (a) unless a concrete consumer is named.
- **Q2 — is a read-only doctor check worth a `cli/` touchpoint at all?** It reads harness config files that "hold other servers' credentials" (Beacon's own words). Default no.
- **Q3 — capture-side privacy.** With Beacon on, every OAC message delivered into a session is candidate trace data and may be forwarded to Beacon Cloud or a SIEM if the operator opted in. That is Beacon's documented behaviour, not an OAC defect, but it changes the residual-risk column for "accidental cross-project disclosure" and "leaked credentials" and must be written down. Does the operator want OAC docs to recommend Beacon's `Metadata-only` privacy mode for OAC-enabled sessions?
- **Q4 — project scoping mismatch.** Beacon memory is per-repository; OAC sessions are per `working_directory` (C4 §5). Two OAC peers in different checkouts will see different memory even for "the same" project. Not OAC's problem to solve, but the docs must not promise otherwise.
- **Q5 — does the operator actually want the out-of-bounds version?** If the real goal is OAC-injected shared context, say so now: that is an ADR-001 amendment decision, not something this epic can absorb quietly.
- **Risk — floating upstream.** Beacon ships often (latest tag `v1.3.29` as of 2026-09-29, with `v1.3.27` and `v1.3.28` immediately preceding it); the pin will move. Since `Gates affected: none`, a pin move here invalidates no gate, but L2's fixtures should record the version they ran on.
- **Risk — MCP era.** Beacon's local server advertises `2024-11-05`; if a harness drops legacy-era MCP, Beacon, not OAC, has to move. Informational.

## Dependencies on existing stages and gates

- L1, L2 (desk), L4 rows, L5 docs, L7: **no stage dependency** — same reasoning as Epic K (planning/decision work outside product paths).
- L3: Stage 2 (Epic E #5), which is blocked on Stage 1 exit (D7, itself blocked on G3's macOS leg) and on the C13 Codex provenance fix. The interface freeze at Stage 2 exit is the last point a content entry can be added without a versioned spec change.
- L5 (`cli/`): Stage 4 (Epic G #7).
- L6: Stage 5 (Epic H #8) and Epic K's driver (#123, reuse contract in K8 #131).
- No gate label applies; this epic depends on no G1-G5 verdict and changes none.
